https://lbpost.com/news/education/kids-m.title: Parents demand answers after students repeatedly suffer headaches, nosebleeds in class
https://lbpost.com/news/education/kids-m.text:
Parents of students temporarily placed at Monroe Elementary School say their kids have been getting mysteriously sick in classrooms. They’re now protesting against the Long Beach Unified School District, saying it did not take their concerns seriously and withheld the full results of environmental tests performed at the school.
Monroe has been closed for more than 13 years, but the Lakewood campus is being used as a temporary site this year for upper grades at nearby Patrick Henry Elementary, which is undergoing renovations. Since moving into the Monroe site in August, students — particularly in one fourth grade classroom — began experiencing headaches, nosebleeds, fatigue and dizziness, according to 10 parents who spoke with the Long Beach Post. In the span of two weeks, the classroom teacher reported dizziness, and four students had nosebleeds, the district said in a letter to families after they raised the alarm.
In response, the school hired an outside company to conduct environmental testing in the classroom, which began on Sept. 30 and revealed high temperatures — reaching 102.6 degrees on the hottest days — and higher than recommended humidity. These conditions “may” explain the symptoms, the report read. The consultant measured low levels of some pollutants, such as carbon monoxide and human-made chemicals like those in paint. And although mold spore levels were also low, the experts recommended retesting because the windows were open, which could skew readings.
Link
Parents said they had to fight for this information, and they’re not satisfied. “They're just keeping us in the dark,” said Ricky Marengo, whose fourth grade daughter has been experiencing headaches. He said parents were sent an email saying the tests hadn't found any ongoing health risks, but it omitted the recommendation for mold retesting. Parents said they learned of that only after one managed to get their hands on the full report.

https://lbpost.com/sponsored/nationally-.text:
Southern California physician leader returns to Long Beach, where his medical career began, to help advance cardiovascular care across MemorialCare.
MemorialCare announced that nationally recognized cardiac surgeon Anthony D. Caffarelli, M.D., has joined MemorialCare as chief of cardiac surgery for the MemorialCare Heart & Vascular Institute and medical director of cardiac surgery at Long Beach Medical Center . In these leadership roles, Dr. Caffarelli will help strengthen the quality, outcomes, and continued growth of cardiovascular care across MemorialCare while advancing cardiac surgery, innovation, research, and patient care throughout Southern California.
“Dr. Caffarelli's appointment reflects MemorialCare's continued investment in expanding access to advanced cardiovascular care across Southern California,” said Elizabeth Acord , vice president, Clinical Institutes, MemorialCare. “He is an accomplished cardiovascular surgeon and respected physician leader whose vision aligns with our commitment to delivering exceptional heart and vascular care. His leadership will help advance the quality, outcomes, and continued growth of the MemorialCare Heart & Vascular Institute, strengthen collaboration across our cardiovascular programs, and expand access to innovative treatments for the patients and communities we serve.”
Dr. Caffarelli has particular expertise in complex aortic procedures, minimally invasive aortic surgery, and mitral valve repair. He performs hundreds of cardiovascular procedures annually and has played a key role in advancing treatment options for patients with complex heart and vascular conditions.

https://lbpost.com/news/no-kings-protest.text:
This article was originally published by LAist on Oct. 16, 2026.
“No Kings” protests are returning for a fourth round Saturday, Oct. 17.
This time, the focus is on the November midterms and getting people prepared to vote. Previous protests had drawn large crowds.
“We expect tens of thousands of people to attend the various No Kings rallies throughout the greater Los Angeles area, and we would not be surprised to see tens of thousands at the downtown rally itself,” said Nick Miller, a press coordinator with 50501 SoCal, a partnering organization.
That protest is taking place at 1 p.m. at Gloria Molina Grand Park.
LAPD said they are aware of the rally and don’t anticipate any issues. Rallies are also being held in Pasadena, Long Beach and Riverside.

https://lbpost.com/hi-lo/long-beach-musi.title: Long Beach Music Museum Pop-Up exhibits artifacts daily during October, with Friday musical receptions, all for free
https://lbpost.com/hi-lo/long-beach-musi.text:
Long Beachers know we have a rich and varied music history, ranging from the Carpenters to blues, jazz and the legendary Snoop Dogg.
A Long Beach Music Museum Pop-Up is offering a month-long celebration of that local musical culture at the Hyatt Regency Long Beach through Oct. 31 — free and open to the public daily, plus Friday evening receptions with food.
View this post on Instagram
A program of the nonprofit Long Beach Blues Society , the pop-up museum is exhibiting collected artifacts reflecting the city’s musical history and culture in “Rocktober @ the Regency.”
Visitors can discover Long Beach music, artists and stories through the exhibits from 11 a.m. to 6 p.m. each day, and experience live music, hors d’oeuvres and beverages during Friday receptions from 5:30 to 7:30 p.m.
The reception this Friday, Oct. 16, features the music of Long Beach band Acoustic Soul Express — comprised of the musical duo Chad Bishop and Ashanti Dykes, bringing a soulful mix of R&B, blues and classic rock — and local saxophonist Daniel Mancuso , beginning at 5:30 p.m.
Arctic Soul Express (Ashanti Dykes, left, and Chad Bishop), are performing Friday, Oct. 16 at the Long Beach Music Museum Pop-Up at the Hyatt Regency. Photo courtesy Long Beach Blues Society.
Musician Bill Grisolia , executive director of the Long Beach Blues Society, founded the organization 10 years ago — growing out of his work for the Long Beach New Blues Festival — with the mission of preserving the legacy of blues through interactive educational programs.
This is the second pop-up for the Long Beach Music Museum. The museum doesn’t yet have a permanent home and this pop-up, like the first one in May, gives visitors an inside look at what such a museum might be like.
The Long Beach Music Museum Pop-Up at the Hyatt Regency. Photo courtesy Malia Koch.

https://lbpost.com/news/crime/police-sho.text:
Body-worn camera footage released this week by the Long Beach Police Department gives the first detailed look at an intense, high-speed shootout that unfolded as officers chased a gunman along the 710 Freeway on Sept. 1.
The Long Beach Post obtained the 35-minute video through a public records request. You can view an edited-down version of it here:
The footage, from the perspective of one officer’s body camera, reveals that a driver fleeing from police fired an AK-47 at police vehicles chasing him. One officer returned fire, shooting through the windshield of the car he was riding in, but did not wound anyone. The chase ultimately ended when the driver exited the freeway in downtown Los Angeles and crashed into a steel fence on South Santa Fe Avenue near East 12th Street, shearing a fire hydrant and sending water shooting up into the underside of his car.
Police were chasing the gunman because of a shooting earlier that night. At about 12:23 a.m., multiple 911 callers reported gunfire in the parking lot behind the Aquarium of the Pacific. The remote area next to the Queens Way Bridge is off Golden Shore, just south of West Shoreline Drive.
One of the callers reported that his “friend” had shot him in the leg with an AK-47, then fled in a silver Honda sedan, according to the 911 call audio.
Another 911 caller said the shooter was “my cousin’s friend” and “we’ve known him for many years,” but didn’t offer any details on what sparked the shooting.

When paramedics arrived in the parking lot, they found three men in their 30s with non-life-threatening gunshot wounds to their lower bodies, according to Long Beach police. Paramedics took two to a hospital and treated one at the scene.
Roughly 20 minutes later, two officers spotted a silver Honda sedan near Pacific Avenue and Burnett Street. When they attempted to pull the car over, the driver fled and entered the northbound 710 Freeway.

https://lbpost.com/eat-see-do-2/eat/litt.title: A Westside baker is feeding her community with backyard crops, free-range eggs and fresh sourdough
https://lbpost.com/eat-see-do-2/eat/litt.text:
It’s said that chickens are considered a gateway drug within the homesteading community: One chicken can lead to a farming addiction. And that was certainly the case for 34-year-old Alyssa Arellano. It started with a couple of chickens and a small garden in the backyard of her Westside home during the pandemic. Now she runs a small-scale farm and sourdough microbakery called Little Arellano Farm .
In her 4,000-square-foot backyard farm, Arellano grows a variety of fresh produce like tomatoes, jalapeños and onions. She also mills her own flour and raises 20 chickens.
Link
The chickens provide all the eggs she uses to bake her sourdough breads and pastries.  Arellano raises a variety of chicken breeds because she says she enjoys collecting the different colored eggs they produce — like brown or blue.
“They're like the millennial new-age Pokemon,” she said. The three newest chickens in her coop are salmon faverolles, which are supposed to lay pink eggs. Those chickens are too young to lay yet, but Arellano is eager to see the eggs.
Two chickens walk past each other while foraging through the garden at the Little Arellano Farm in the Westside neighborhood of Long Beach on Tuesday, Oct. 6, 2026. Owner Alyssa Arellano keeps 20 chickens and uses their eggs for her baking. Photo by Thomas R. Cordova.
Arellano grew up in San Pedro and the Central Valley. She started baking with her mom at 3 years old, sitting on the counter smashing bananas for banana bread to put in Christmas baskets. As the treats baked, Arellano said she and her mom would dance and sing in the kitchen.
“That was like the best time of my life.”
But at 14, Arellano’s father died suddenly from a heart attack, and baking became an outlet for her grief.

https://lbpost.com/eat-see-do-2/see/land.title: Long Beach Landmark Theatre to stage ‘A Man of No Importance’ beginning this weekend
https://lbpost.com/eat-see-do-2/see/land.text:
As its title suggests, “A Man of No Importance” — beginning a three-week run this weekend at the Long Beach Landmark Theatre — is not a flashy musical, but it portrays profound depths.
Alfie Byrne is a bus conductor in 1964 Dublin who has a secret. Moreover, he has a poetic spirit and gets local townspeople to stage amateur plays in their church hall.
But when Alfie decides to stage his dream play, “Salome” — written by his favorite writer, Oscar Wilde, nearly 70 years before — the town’s Catholic conservatives decide its seductive scenes are morally degenerate and want to ban its production.
In trying to persuade them otherwise, Alfie has imaginary conversations with the flamboyant Wilde and becomes emboldened to reveal more of himself, risking consequences both physical and emotional.
Winner of the 2003 Outer Critics Circle Award for Best Off-Broadway Musical , “A Man of No Importance” is written by Terrence McNally, with music by Stephen Flaherty and lyrics by Lynn Ahrens, based on a 1994 film of the same name. This is the same trio behind the Tony Award-winning 1998 Broadway musical “Ragtime.”
Curtis Heard, music director of the theater, is conducting a live orchestra for the show’s Irish-inflected score. And a cast of nearly 20 will bring the play to life — directed and choreographed by artistic director Megan O’Toole, who will also play the role of Mrs. Patrick.
Mark Wheeler plays the role of Oscar Wilde in Long Beach Landmark Theatre's upcoming “A Man of No Importance.” Photo by Lisa Bode Heard.
The show will perform at the First Congregational Church of Long Beach like the theater’s previous productions, including last year’s musically spectacular “ Jagged Little Pill ,” enhanced by the building’s acoustics.
With a church conflict at the center of “A Man of No Importance,” the setting is not only fitting, but makes it more metatheatrical — a play staged in a church about staging a play in a church.

https://lbpost.com/news/affordable-housi.title: He promised homes for families. Now he’s accused of millions in fraud — and one attorney says that’s just the beginning
https://lbpost.com/news/affordable-housi.text:
An affordable housing charity that controls hundreds of apartments in Long Beach is facing a torrent of accusations that it cheated the government out of tens of millions of dollars, defrauded homeless assistance programs and swindled low-income tenants out of money.
The nonprofit Helpful Housing and its for-profit subsidiary Ocean Structure are run by Rodney Rosenstein, who is in federal custody after being indicted in connection with a series of alleged fraud schemes in Arizona.
In Long Beach, a flood of similar accusations at 15 residential complexes has gone virtually unnoticed until now. They are spread across dozens of lawsuits reviewed by the Long Beach Post, as well as through obtained property records, financial documents, a whistleblower account from a former employee and interviews with tenants. Separately, they are little more than small-time court cases, rental disputes and loan defaults. Taken together, they allege Rosenstein is at the center of a cascading scam that took advantage of multimillion-dollar homeless services programs and federal affordable housing incentives with little oversight.
One attorney in particular managed to build the most comprehensive view of the alleged scheme while she pursued a maintenance worker’s wage-theft case. Kimberly Lind says Rosenstein’s organization falsified paperwork under the city’s nose for years, all to hide a system of overcharging agencies that placed formerly unhoused people in the apartments.
The full extent of the potential fraud in Long Beach — which also included low-income tenants alleging they were charged exorbitant fees without cause — remains unknown.
Lawyers for Rosenstein declined to comment or did not respond to detailed questions from the Post. The city of Long Beach has said the Arizona indictment “raises new concerns” about its dealings with Rosenstein’s organizations, and it’s already suing him over missing payments on federal loans that it administers.

https://lbpost.com/news/song-tate-memori.title: As police searched for driver who killed beloved grandma, neighbors moved swiftly to support her family
https://lbpost.com/news/song-tate-memori.text:
After an outpouring of support, the daughter of a Long Beach woman killed by a hit-and-run driver is extending an open invitation for neighbors to attend the celebration of life for her mother, Song Tate.
It just made sense, said daughter Sonya Rose. She has leaned heavily on the people around her while police search for the driver who hit 72-year-old Tate last month on Long Beach Boulevard.
Without their support, “I wouldn’t be where I’m at mentally right now,” she said.
So, this Sunday from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m., Rose's family will hold a memorial for her mother, and anyone who would like to attend should message her via Instagram for the location.
Visitors are encouraged to wear emerald green, her mom’s favorite color.
View this post on Instagram
After her mom’s death, Rose has heard from countless neighbors who have come by to pay their respects. Most said they knew Tate from her habit of making sure people around the neighborhood had enough to eat .
Recently, while getting lunch at StormBurger in North Long Beach, Rose stumbled into more support.
One of the store managers, whom she had worked with previously, offered to put together a fundraiser on her behalf. Details for that event are forthcoming.
Rose is still piecing together what happened on the night her mother died. Police have not caught the driver, but recently released an image of the suspected vehicle .
Link
Security camera footage showed the car in a parking lot near Willow Street and Long Beach Boulevard before the crash, which happened at about 8:52 p.m. on Sept. 5, according to Long Beach police.
The driver was heading eastbound on Willow Street before turning southbound onto Long Beach Boulevard. After the crash, the car — a silver Ford Mustang with a black convertible top, black stripes and black rims — was last spotted heading southbound on Pasadena Avenue near 20th Street.

https://lbpost.com/news/education/hazing.title: High school water polo players hurt in ‘shocking’ hazing incident, coach says in email to parents
https://lbpost.com/news/education/hazing.text:
Members of the Wilson High School boys’ water polo team subjected some of their teammates to violent hazing in a San Jose-area hotel room Friday, according to an email from the head coach to the team’s parents.
The email from Coach Zac Polmanteer — which a parent provided to the Long Beach Post — says the top-ranked varsity water polo team was traveling to compete in a tournament over the weekend when, after securing two wins on the first day of competition, most of the team convened in one hotel room that night. There, “multiple student athletes were subjected to humiliating and physically harmful acts. Some athletes sustained injuries from being physically struck by their teammates,” Polmanteer wrote. He did not disclose the extent of the injuries.
Polmanteer wrote that he was informed the next day about noise complaints from the room where the team had gathered and he warned them about “breaking of curfew and general team conduct,” but he did not learn about the hazing until returning to Long Beach on Sunday evening. In the email, sent Monday night, he emphasized the gravity of the situation.
Link
“This level of behavior is shocking, unacceptable, and completely contrary to everything we stand for as a program,” he wrote. Polmanteer did not respond to requests for comment from the Post.
On Monday, athletes who traveled on the trip were interviewed individually during practice hours and questioned by the school’s athletic director and several water polo coaches, the email read.
Based on the interviews, the school administration and coaching staff devised consequences — including suspension from school and water polo — and a plan of action to ensure “these events never occur again,” according to the email.
“Hazing is a cultural problem, even when only a handful of athletes directly participate. You can distinguish individual responsibility while acknowledging that the entire program has a responsibility to maintain a safe environment,” Polmanteer wrote.
